lead: A power diode is the simplest power switch: it conducts when its anode is positive and blocks when it is negative, with no control terminal. It is not ideal: on, it drops about a volt; off, it leaks a little; and at turn-off it conducts backwards for a moment while its stored charge is removed. That reverse recovery decides which diode can work at which switching frequency. Power diodes sit in every rectifier and in the freewheeling paths of choppers and inverters.
prereq: You need: the PN junction diode (forward bias, reverse bias, depletion region).

sections.h3: Structure and the static V–I curve

blocks.text: A power diode has three layers: a heavily doped p<sup>+</sup> anode (A), a lightly doped n<sup>−</sup> drift region and a heavily doped n<sup>+</sup> cathode (K). The drift region is wide and lightly doped because it holds the reverse voltage. The current is i<sub>D</sub> and v<sub>D</sub> is measured from A to K.

Forward bias: almost no current flows until v<sub>D</sub> passes the threshold (cut-in) voltage V<sub>TO</sub>, about 0.7 V to 0.8 V for silicon. Above it the curve is nearly a straight line of slope 1/r<sub>d</sub>, because holes and electrons flood the drift region and lower its resistance (conductivity modulation). At rated current the drop is usually 1 V to 1.5 V.

where v<sub>D</sub> is the on-state voltage (V), V<sub>TO</sub> the threshold voltage (V), i<sub>D</sub> the forward current (A) and r<sub>d</sub> the slope resistance (Ω). The average conduction loss is then P<sub>cond</sub> = V<sub>TO</sub> I<sub>avg</sub> + r<sub>d</sub> I<sub>rms</sub>², with I<sub>avg</sub> and I<sub>rms</sub> the average and rms diode currents.

Reverse bias: only a small leakage current I<sub>R</sub> flows until the breakdown voltage V<sub>BR</sub>. The datasheet's V<sub>RRM</sub>, the repetitive peak reverse voltage, lies below V<sub>BR</sub>. An ideal switch would have zero drop, zero leakage and zero switching time; the real diode has V<sub>TO</sub> and r<sub>d</sub>, I<sub>R</sub>, and a turn-off delay from stored charge.
Turn-on: for a short forward recovery time t<sub>fr</sub> the drift region is not yet flooded with carriers, so the voltage overshoots its steady value.

Turn-off: the circuit forces the current down at a rate di/dt set by the supply voltage and circuit inductance. The current passes zero, but stored charge keeps the junction conducting, so the current goes negative. After t<sub>a</sub> it reaches the peak reverse recovery current I<sub>RRM</sub>; then the junction blocks and the current returns to zero in t<sub>b</sub>. The reverse recovery time is t<sub>rr</sub> = t<sub>a</sub> + t<sub>b</sub>, and the area of the negative pulse is the reverse recovery charge Q<sub>rr</sub>.

the triangle approximation, with Q<sub>rr</sub> in coulombs, I<sub>RRM</sub> in amperes and t<sub>rr</sub> in seconds. Because the current falls at the circuit's di/dt until the peak, I<sub>RRM</sub> ≈ t<sub>a</sub> × di/dt.

The softness factor is S = t<sub>b</sub> / t<sub>a</sub>. A snappy diode (S well below 1) stops its reverse current abruptly, and the circuit inductance turns that into a voltage spike and ringing. Recovery also costs energy: the recovery current flows while the switch turning on still holds most of the supply voltage V<sub>s</sub>, so the loss is about P<sub>rr</sub> ≈ Q<sub>rr</sub> V<sub>s</sub> f<sub>s</sub> at switching frequency f<sub>s</sub>, and most of it heats the switch.

Typical reverse recovery
Where it is used
rows: under about 5 µs, down to tens of ns

blocks.text: A Schottky diode is a metal–semiconductor junction with only majority carriers, so it drops about 0.3 V to 0.5 V and has almost no recovery, but silicon Schottky diodes block only up to about 100 V to 200 V. Silicon carbide Schottky diodes reach 600 V to 1700 V (see wide band-gap devices). The circuits are taught under rectifiers, DC-DC converters, inverters and AC-AC converters.

examples.question: A diode carrying 10 A is turned off with di/dt = 8 A/µs; it has I<sub>RRM</sub> = 8 A and t<sub>rr</sub> = 2 µs. Find t<sub>a</sub>, t<sub>b</sub>, the softness factor S and Q<sub>rr</sub>. If the diode blocks V<sub>s</sub> = 300 V and switches at f<sub>s</sub> = 20 kHz, estimate the recovery loss P<sub>rr</sub>.
steps: Time to reach the reverse peak: t<sub>a</sub> = I<sub>RRM</sub> / (di/dt) = 8 A ÷ 8 A/µs = 1 µs.
Recovery tail: t<sub>b</sub> = t<sub>rr</sub> − t<sub>a</sub> = 2 µs − 1 µs = 1 µs, so S = t<sub>b</sub> / t<sub>a</sub> = 1 ÷ 1 = 1 (a soft diode).
Charge: Q<sub>rr</sub> = ½ × I<sub>RRM</sub> × t<sub>rr</sub> = 0.5 × 8 A × 2 × 10<sup>−6</sup> s = 8 × 10<sup>−6</sup> C = 8 µC.
Loss: P<sub>rr</sub> ≈ Q<sub>rr</sub> V<sub>s</sub> f<sub>s</sub> = 8 × 10<sup>−6</sup> C × 300 V × 20 × 10<sup>3</sup> Hz = 48 W.
examples.answer: t<sub>a</sub> = 1 µs, t<sub>b</sub> = 1 µs, S = 1, Q<sub>rr</sub> = 8 µC and P<sub>rr</sub> ≈ 48 W.

examples.question: The same diode conducts its 10 A for half of each cycle (duty ratio 0.5). It has V<sub>TO</sub> = 0.85 V and r<sub>d</sub> = 12 mΩ. Find its conduction loss and compare it with the 48 W of recovery loss. What changes if a fast-recovery diode with I<sub>RRM</sub> = 2 A and t<sub>rr</sub> = 0.2 µs is used?
steps: On-state drop at 10 A: v<sub>D</sub> = 0.85 + 10 × 0.012 = 0.97 V.
Average and rms currents: I<sub>avg</sub> = 10 × 0.5 = 5 A; I<sub>rms</sub>² = 10² × 0.5 = 50 A².
P<sub>cond</sub> = V<sub>TO</sub> I<sub>avg</sub> + r<sub>d</sub> I<sub>rms</sub>² = 0.85 × 5 + 0.012 × 50 = 4.25 + 0.60 = 4.85 W (check: 0.97 V × 10 A × 0.5 = 4.85 W).
Fast-recovery diode: Q<sub>rr</sub> = 0.5 × 2 A × 0.2 µs = 0.2 µC, so P<sub>rr</sub> = 0.2 × 10<sup>−6</sup> × 300 × 20 000 = 1.2 W.
examples.answer: P<sub>cond</sub> = 4.85 W against P<sub>rr</sub> = 48 W; the fast-recovery diode cuts the recovery loss to 1.2 W.

traps: Reverse recovery is a turn-off effect. Do not add t<sub>rr</sub> to the turn-on time.

Q<sub>rr</sub> is a charge (µC), I<sub>RRM</sub> is a current (A). Q<sub>rr</sub> = ½ I<sub>RRM</sub> t<sub>rr</sub>, not I<sub>RRM</sub> t<sub>rr</sub>: forgetting the ½ doubles the answer (16 µC instead of 8 µC).
V<sub>TO</sub> is the threshold, not the drop at rated current. Using 0.85 V instead of 0.97 V at 10 A under-reads the conduction loss.

quiz.q: Define reverse recovery time t<sub>rr</sub> of a power diode.
quiz.a: t<sub>rr</sub> is the time from the instant the diode current passes through zero at turn-off until the reverse current has decayed to a small specified value (often 25 % of I<sub>RRM</sub>); t<sub>rr</sub> = t<sub>a</sub> + t<sub>b</sub>.

quiz.q: Why does a diode carry reverse current for a short time after the circuit tries to turn it off?
quiz.a: Minority carriers stored in the drift region during conduction keep the junction conducting. Until this charge is swept out or recombines, the junction cannot block, so current flows backwards; its peak is I<sub>RRM</sub>.

quiz.q: A diode has I<sub>RRM</sub> = 6 A and t<sub>rr</sub> = 3 µs. Find Q<sub>rr</sub>, and P<sub>rr</sub> when it blocks 200 V at 25 kHz.
A rectifier diode has V<sub>TO</sub> = 0.8 V and r<sub>d</sub> = 5 mΩ. It carries I<sub>avg</sub> = 20 A with I<sub>rms</sub> = 31.4 A. Find its conduction loss.
A designer replaces a fast-recovery diode in a 50 kHz chopper with a cheaper general-purpose diode of the same current rating. Predict what happens.
quiz.a: Its t<sub>rr</sub> is microseconds, so Q<sub>rr</sub> and P<sub>rr</sub> ≈ Q<sub>rr</sub> V<sub>s</sub> f<sub>s</sub> are many times larger, mostly as extra turn-on loss in the transistor, which overheats; the large reverse current also raises interference.

beyond: Not for the exam. Silicon carbide Schottky diodes have almost no recovery charge, so they are now standard in power-factor-correction stages, fast chargers and solar inverters. Search for ‘soft recovery diode’ and ‘SiC Schottky diode’.
